# Deep Learning Model for Differentiating Thyroid Eye Disease and Orbital Myositis on Computed Tomography (CT) Imaging

**Authors:** Sierra K. Ha; Lisa Y. Lin; Min Shi; Mengyu Wang; Ji Yun Han; Nahyoung Grace Lee

**Affiliations:** 1Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA. | 2Ophthalmic Plastic Surgery Service, Department of Ophthalmology, Massachusetts Eye and Ear, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA. | 3Harvard Ophthalmology AI Lab, Schepens Eye Research Institute of Massachusetts Eye and Ear, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA. | 4The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University, Providence, RI

## Abstract

To develop a deep learning model using orbital computed tomography (CT) imaging to accurately distinguish thyroid eye disease (TED) and orbital myositis, two conditions with overlapping clinical presentations.

Retrospective, single-center cohort study spanning 12 years including normal controls, TED, and orbital myositis patients with orbital imaging and examination by an oculoplastic surgeon. A deep learning model employing a Visual Geometry Group-16 network was trained on various binary combinations of TED, orbital myositis, and controls using single slices of coronal orbital CT images.

A total of 1628 images from 192 patients (110 TED, 51 orbital myositis, 31 controls) were included. The primary model comparing orbital myositis and TED had accuracy of 98.4% and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.999. In detecting orbital myositis, it had a sensitivity, specificity, and F1 score of 0.964, 0.994, and 0.984, respectively.

Deep learning models can differentiate TED and orbital myositis based on a single, coronal orbital CT image with high accuracy. Their ability to distinguish these conditions based not only on extraocular muscle enlargement but also other salient features suggests potential applications in diagnostics and treatment beyond these conditions.

## Introduction

Thyroid eye disease (TED) and orbital myositis are two distinct orbital pathologies which may present with overlapping clinical presentations. Both conditions commonly manifest with symptoms such as orbital pain, diplopia, and proptosis. Differentiation of these diseases is crucial to initiate appropriate treatment and prevent complications such as permanent disability or vision loss. Diagnosis and subsequent treatment may be delayed if the patient first presents to a non-ophthalmologist or oculoplastic specialist. Orbital computed tomography (CT) plays a significant role in diagnosing these conditions and is utilized in various settings. It may reveal distinct features typical of orbital myositis, such as unilateral enhancement of extraocular muscles and their tendinous insertions.1 In contrast, TED may present as either unilateral or bilateral and rarely involves the lateral rectus muscle or extraocular muscle tendons.2 Recognizing subtle differences between these conditions is crucial for tailoring effective treatment strategies.

The advent of deep learning has revolutionized medical diagnostics, demonstrating remarkable progress across various medical specialties. In the field of oculoplastic surgery, recent studies have employed deep learning to assess and diagnose orbital and eyelid conditions using diverse imaging modalities such as CT, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and external photographs.3–5 This technological advancement has shown promise in streamlining clinical decision-making processes and optimizing surgical strategies. Many studies have focused in particular on the use of artificial intelligence in diagnosing TED, using this technology to predict clinical activity and severity.6–8

The authors have previously demonstrated the efficacy of a deep learning model that utilizes CT imaging to distinguish TED with and without clinical signs of compressive optic neuropathy.9 This model is based on the Visual Geometry Group (VGG)-16 convolutional neural network, a widely used deep learning architecture for image classification and feature extraction. VGG-16 consists of 16 layers with pre-trained weights which enable it to learn hierarchical and complex spatial patterns, making it well-suited for detecting subtle differences in medical imaging. In comparison to an ophthalmologist presented with solely imaging without additional clinical data, the model was more accurate in distinguishing TED with and without compressive optic neuropathy (89.5% versus 70%). However, the ability of this model to distinguish TED from other etiologies of orbital inflammation causing enlarged extraocular muscles, such as orbital myositis, has not yet been explored. This distinction is crucial for practical applications in clinical triage, diagnosis, and subsequent treatment planning, as TED and orbital myositis may both present with vague orbital pain but may require different medical approaches. Therefore, in this study, the authors sought to develop a deep learning model to accurately differentiate between TED and orbital myositis based on orbital CT imaging. This model will contribute to the refinement of clinical decision-making processes by offering a tool to enhance the accuracy and efficiency of diagnosis and subsequent therapeutic strategies for various orbital pathologies.

## Materials and Methods

This study was a retrospective cohort study of patients with TED and orbital myositis at Massachusetts Eye and Ear (MEE), a tertiary ophthalmic institution, from a 12-year period (August 2011 to 2023). The study was conducted in accordance with the tenets set forth in the Declaration of Helsinki, and all necessary authorizations were obtained from the institutional review board at Massachusetts General Brigham (MGB). The requirement for informed consent was waived due to the retrospective nature of the study. Subjects included patients greater than 18 years of age with a CT scan of the orbit who had a complete examination by an oculoplastic surgeon within 3 months of the scan being performed. Patients were included if they had a documented diagnosis of either orbital myositis or TED in the electronic medical record. Clinician diagnosis was based on a comprehensive assessment, including clinical examination, imaging, and relevant laboratory testing. Exclusion criteria included patients with other diagnoses, such as trauma, tumors, or other inflammatory processes, or any history of prior orbital surgeries (e.g., orbital decompressions). In cases of orbital myositis, patients with concurrent dacryoadenitis were included due to the frequent co-occurrence of these conditions in clinical practice, whereas those with additional inflammatory processes were excluded. For comparison, patients with a normal orbital CT scan and no history of orbital disease were used as normal controls.

Patient data was collected as previously described.9 Demographic characteristics, clinical history, and clinical examination findings by an oculoplastic surgeon performed closest to the date of the CT were obtained from the electronic medical record. Subjects were divided into four groups: normal controls, TED without optic neuropathy (ON), TED with ON, and orbital myositis. As per previously described protocol,9 TED with ON was defined as the presence of clinical signs, including dyschromatopsia, Humphrey visual field changes consistent with TED, relative afferent pupillary defect, and/or optic nerve changes on clinical exam. Each orbit was characterized separately due to the asymmetry of TED and orbital myositis. These groups were considered as the ground truth for training the deep learning model.

### Data Preprocessing

In order to evaluate the effectiveness of the deep learning model in identifying thyroid eye disease (TED) and orbital myositis, single, discrete images of the orbital region of interest were manually cropped from coronal CT scans and processed per the protocol described previously.9 In brief, the cropped area was confined to the outer limits of the bony orbital walls for each orbit. Only coronal slices including the area from the insertion of the optic nerve up to the orbital apex were analyzed. All image samples were resized to 256 x 256 pixels and converted into 3-channel Red Green Blue images by applying colormap processing, which mapped grayscale intensity values to a predefined gradient, enhancing compatibility with the adopted deep learning model. The analysis was performed separately for the right and left orbits of TED and control patients, while only the affected orbit of orbital myositis patients was analyzed. The 2-dimensional region of interest (ROI) images were then categorized into four predetermined groups as described above (normal controls, TED without ON, TED with ON, and orbital myositis).

### Model Training and Evaluation

The deep learning model for predicting TED versus orbital myositis status was trained using the VGG-16 network, which was pre-trained on ImageNet data to initialize the model.10 Experimental settings included: (1) VGG-16 trained for all TED (with or without ON) versus orbital myositis, (2) VGG-16 trained for normal controls and orbital myositis, (3) VGG-16 trained for TED without ON and orbital myositis, (4) VGG-16 trained for TED with ON and orbital myositis, (5) VGG-16 trained for all TED and a subset of orbital myositis patients with sole involvement of the lateral rectus muscle, (6) VGG-16 trained for all TED and a subset of orbital myositis excluding those with sole involvement of the lateral rectus muscle. Experimental settings (5) and (6) were designed to test the hypothesis that the deep learning model may rely on determination of specific extraocular muscle involvement to differentiate these conditions (e.g. lack of lateral rectus involvement in TED versus possibility of involvement of lateral rectus in orbital myositis). For each experimental setting, 80% of data was randomly sampled and used for training the deep learning model, and the remaining 20% of data was used for testing the deep learning model’s performance. The adopted deep learning framework for TED and orbital myositis disease status prediction based on the VGG-16 network was adopted from the framework employed previously in developing a model to predict thyroid eye disease status (Supplementary Figure 1).9 In the current study, the input to the model comprised a 256 x 256 x 3 RGB image, and were similarly subjected to five convolutional blocks for feature extraction. The output of the fifth block achieved a densely connected layer and a dropout layer. The dense layer was a singular scalar, enabling binary-class prediction through a sigmoid function transformation.

The pre-trained VGG-16 model applied to the current data set underwent further refinement with 100 epochs and a mini-batch size of 8. Root Mean Square Propagation (RMSProp) was adopted for optimization of a binary cross-entropy loss.11,12 Throughout the training process, the learning rate was set at 0.00001. This comprehensive architecture, rooted in the VGG-16 network, was deliberately adopted for its efficacy in handling the complexities inherent in predicting the status of thyroid eye disease and orbital myositis.

### Statistical Analysis

Statistical analysis was performed using RStudio Version 2023.12.1+402. Demographics and clinical characteristics were described using traditional descriptive methods. Evaluation of the model was based on accuracy, precision, sensitivity, specificity, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and sample-weighted F1 score in each of the experimental settings described above. F1 score, a metric for deep learning model performance calculated as the harmonic mean of precision and recall, was weighted based on sample size in order to account for class-imbalances in data distribution.13

## Results

A total of 243 eyes from 192 patients met inclusion criteria for the current study, including 32 eyes from 31 normal controls, 84 eyes from 83 TED without ON patients, 76 eyes from 40 TED with ON patients, and 51 eyes from 51 orbital myositis patients. Thirteen patients were included in both the TED without ON and TED with ON groups because they had one eye meeting criteria for optic neuropathy. Within the TED group, most eyes demonstrated enlargement of multiple muscles, including the inferior, medial, and superior rectus muscles, while no eyes demonstrated enlargement of the lateral rectus. Among the orbital myositis patients, single-muscle enlargement was more common, with 13 eyes from 13 patients demonstrating sole involvement of the lateral rectus muscle. In total, 1,628 discrete images were obtained and processed, and included 373 images of normal controls, 459 images of TED without ON, 355 images of TED with ON, and 441 images of orbital myositis. The median age of all participants was 64 years (range: 19 – 91 years). The median age across the different subgroups was significantly different (p < 0.05) with younger patients in the orbital myositis group (median: 46, interquartile range (IQR): 19–88). Most patients were female (68%) and of white race (82%). While all of the TED patients exhibited bilateral disease, the majority of the orbital myositis patients (98%) exhibited unilateral disease. Baseline characteristics of the subjects are further summarized in Table 1.

Results of binary modeling performed between groups are illustrated in Table 2. The primary model distinguished between all TED and orbital myositis with an overall accuracy of 98.4% and AUC of 0.999. In detecting orbital myositis, it had a precision of 98.8%, sensitivity of 96.4% and specificity of 99.4%. Sample-weighted F1 score for the overall model was 0.984. The model misclassified 3 orbital myositis images as TED and 1 TED image as orbital myositis (Figure 1A).

For experiments (2) through (4) comparing other combinations of normal, TED without ON, and TED with ON versus orbital myositis, the model achieved accuracies ranging from 98.1% to 98.8% with AUC ranging from 0.996 to 0.999 and F1 score ranging from 0.981 to 0.988 (Table 2). The model misclassified 1 orbital myositis as normal, 1 normal as orbital myositis, 3 orbital myositis as TED without ON, 1 orbital myositis as TED with ON, and 2 TED with ON as orbital myositis (Figure 1B–D).

The model trained on TED versus orbital myositis with sole involvement of the lateral rectus muscle (orbital myositis LR) achieved an accuracy of 99.5%, AUC of 0.994, sensitivity of 94.7% and specificity of 100%. It misclassified 1 orbital myositis LR image as TED (Figure 2A). The model trained on TED versus orbital myositis excluding those with sole involvement of the lateral rectus muscle (orbital myositis non-LR) achieved an accuracy of 95.6%, AUC of 0.996, sensitivity 92.6%, and specificity of 96.9%. The model misclassified 3 orbital myositis non-LR images as TED and 5 TED images as orbital myositis non-LR (Figure 2B, Figure 3C).

## Discussion

This is the first study, to the authors’ knowledge, to evaluate the use of deep learning to distinguish TED from another orbital inflammatory condition on CT imaging. The findings demonstrate that a deep learning model can accurately differentiate between TED and orbital myositis based on a single slice of an orbital CT image with high accuracy, AUC, and F1 score of 98.4%, 0.999, and 0.984, respectively. The model also performed well across various combinations of TED without ON, TED with ON, and normal controls versus orbital myositis, with accuracy rates of 98.3%, 98.1%, and 98.8%, respectively (AUC range: 0.996 to 0.999). The model remained highly accurate regardless of the particular muscles involved in orbital myositis, suggesting that important features leveraged by the model include but are not limited to specific extraocular muscle involvement.

The analysis of the misclassified images revealed that the model is less accurate in detecting atypical presentations of the diseases. For example, in Figure 3A, the single image orbital myositis image that was incorrectly classified as normal lack the expected features of orbital myositis, such as enlargement of a single extraocular muscle.14 Similarly, two TED with ON images misclassified as orbital myositis lack the typical severity of muscle enlargement and optic nerve compression, crucial diagnostic features of TED with ON (Figure 3B).15 The absence of these classic features in the misclassified images suggests that the model may struggle with cases that do not fit the typical presentation profile. Additionally, the model’s accuracy decreases when images contain features consistent with the alternative disorder. For example, one of the 2 TED with ON images misclassified as orbital myositis demonstrates sole muscle involvement of the superior rectus muscle (Figure 3B). This is notable because TED typically involves multiple extraocular muscles, whereas orbital myositis more frequently presents with isolated involvement of a single muscle.2 Reassuringly, although the model is less accurate at detecting atypical presentations of disease, it remains highly effective in distinguishing TED with ON and orbital myositis, with few misclassifications. The ability to differentiate these two groups is particularly important clinically, as TED with ON would require more urgent referral to an oculoplastic surgeon for intervention.16

Other studies have also demonstrated the ability of neural networks and deep learning models to diagnose TED based on CT imaging. One such model differentiated between normal and TED CT scans with accuracy of 87% (AUC 0.919).17 Another model that stratified TED based on severity distinguished normal versus TED without ON and normal versus TED with ON, with AUC of 0.826 and 0.930 and accuracy of 0.895 and 0.979, respectively.6 The authors of the current study have also previously described the use of a deep learning model for accurately detecting TED along with clinical signs of optic neuropathy based on orbital CT, including when compared with human expert grading.9 However, all of these studies thus far have excluded any patients with a history of other orbital disorders or orbital inflammation. The current study further elaborates on the utility of our group’s previously developed deep learning model and prior studies by demonstrating the ability to differentiate TED from orbital conditions that present with similar findings. This would be a more clinically relevant tool for a clinician, particularly those less familiar with orbital diseases. However, given this updated model has not yet been directly compared to clinician performance, further studies are warranted to validate its use as a clinical screening tool. Future efforts may also explore this model’s performance in atypical patient presentations of orbital myositis which have been reported, such as patients with orbital myositis with features mimicking TED,18 or in cases of orbital myositis that develop in patients with a history of TED.19

The involvement of different extraocular muscles in TED and orbital myositis aids in their distinction. TED most commonly affects the inferior rectus, followed by the medial rectus, superior rectus, and least commonly the lateral rectus.2 In contrast, orbital myositis predominantly affects the medial, lateral, or superior rectus muscles.20 In the current study, the performance of the deep learning model was studied via scenarios contingent on the specific extraocular muscles involved. Notably, when comparing all instances of TED against orbital myositis with exclusive lateral rectus involvement, the model demonstrated an accuracy of 99.5%, F1 score of 0.995 and AUC of 0.994. Similarly, in the comparison excluding cases with sole lateral rectus involvement, the accuracy remained robust at 95.6%, with an F1 score of 0.956, and AUC of 0.996. While the heightened accuracy in the scenario with sole lateral rectus muscle involvement may be due to the model’s emphasis on extraocular muscle involvement, the sustained accuracy in the absence of this specificity hints at the utilization of additional discriminative features. This suggests that the model can effectively distinguish between these conditions even without the exclusive presence of lateral rectus pathology. This underscores the model’s versatility and ability to leverage various characteristics for accurate classification.

Review of the misclassified images from the experimental settings comparing extraocular muscle involvement demonstrates that some of the orbital myositis images falsely predicted as TED involve multiple extraocular muscles, a feature more common in TED than in orbital myositis (Figure 3C). Similarly to the misclassifications in the other binary comparisons described above, this suggests that the developed model may be less accurate in identifying atypical presentations of disease, though this has minimal effect on the overall performance of the model. The precision in scenarios involving specific muscle involvement indicates potential broader applications of this method in discerning other causes of extraocular muscle enlargement, such as immunoglobulin G4-related disease ophthalmic disease, which preferentially affect the lateral rectus muscle,21 and lymphoma and sarcoidosis, which have been demonstrated to affect the superior rectus.22,23 Other studies have examined the enlargement of extraocular muscles via assessment of muscle thickness with deep neural network in diagnosing TED, reporting AUC of 0.946.24 Future endeavors could aim to enhance predictive accuracy by integrating both the estimation of extraocular muscle enlargement and the identification of the specific muscle involved, a comprehensive approach to optimize the predictive capacity of the model in discerning various etiologies of extraocular muscle enlargement.

While the results of experimental settings (5) all TED versus a subset of orbital myositis patients with sole involvement of the lateral rectus muscle and (6) all TED versus a subset of orbital myositis excluding those with sole involvement of the lateral rectus muscle suggest the significance of extraocular muscle involvement in the model’s decision-making process, a limitation that remains is the inability to comprehend the other features recognized by the learning algorithm. While clinicians may rely on features such as differences in muscle involvement, muscle enhancement, and orbital fat stranding to distinguish orbital myositis from TED, in the current study, it cannot be concluded what features are learned by the deep learning model. Future efforts will address this limitation by transforming the model into an explainable machine learning model, using methods for feature importance analysis such as SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and saliency mapping to enhance the applicability of the model in clinical settings.25,26 Incorporating explainable deep learning into the current model could enable clinicians to understand how the model arrives at its decisions, improving transparency and fostering trust in its diagnostic capabilities. Additionally, elucidating the salient features learned by the model could help to further refine understanding of the underlying pathophysiology of TED and orbital myositis, potentially leading to new insights and therapeutic strategies. Furthermore, the limited ability of the model to recognize differences in TED versus orbital myositis may be due to the fact the fusiform extraocular muscle enlargement in TED may be easier to distinguish from diffuse enlargement of muscle in myositis in the axial plane compared to the coronal plane analyzed in this study. Further studies may incorporate multiple views or more comprehensive volumetric analyses in order to better distinguish these characteristics.

There are several limitations of this study that warrant consideration. While steps were taken to mitigate degradation and overfitting during the model training process, including the use of dropout layers, a low learning rate, and RMSProp optimization, future refinements could incorporate additional regularization techniques such as data augmentation or cross-validation to further enhance model stability and applicability to diverse clinical settings. However, even with these improvements, the model’s performance remains contingent on the population and conditions it is trained on. For instance, the exclusion of patients with enlarged extraocular muscles due to etiologies other than TED and orbital myositis restricts the model’s applicability in clinical practice. Additionally, the small sample size, single-center setting, and predominantly white patient population may limit generalizability of the findings. While our sample included 191 patients, this sample size is similar to that of other studies which have demonstrated the use of deep learning for diagnosing TED on CT imaging with cohorts ranging from 141 to 432 patients.6,8,9,24,27 Baseline demographics differed in the orbital myositis group, with generally younger patients and a larger proportion of male patients, as compared to all other groups. Although the proportion of white patients across the groups did not differ significantly, the application of the model to a more diverse population may be limited because of potential variability in orbital anatomy among different races and ethnicities.28,29 To address these limitations, future iterations of the model should integrate additional testing, demographic data, and clinical information and include training and validation on a larger and more diverse sample to enhance its diagnostic capabilities and broaden its scope.

This study demonstrates the use of deep learning technology for the precise differentiation of thyroid eye disease (TED) and orbital myositis through analysis of orbital CT imaging. The study’s strength lies not only in its comprehensive patient cohort over a 12-year period but also in its approach of comparing TED with a different type of orbital inflammation. This approach enhances the applicability of the technology and its potential to improve clinical diagnostics in oculoplastic surgery. The study’s broader applications extend beyond TED and orbital myositis, suggesting the potential for this deep learning model to contribute to the earlier detection of various orbital conditions, including those with specific extraocular muscle involvement. These findings pave the way for continued refinement and implementation of deep learning models in clinical settings, ultimately benefiting patients by improving accuracy and efficiency in the screening of thyroid eye disease and related orbital disorders.

# Endocrine mucin-producing sweat gland carcinoma of the eyelid in an elderly male: A case report

**Authors:** Sierra K Ha; Anania Woldetensaye; Ryanne A Brown; Kelsey E Hirotsu; Benyam Kinde

**Affiliations:** aHarvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | bByers Eye Institute, Stanford University School of Medicine, Palo Alto, CA, USA | cDepartment of Dermatology, Stanford University School of Medicine, Redwood City, CA, USA | dDepartment of Pathology, Stanford University School of Medicine, Palo Alto, CA, USA

## Abstract

To report a rare case of endocrine mucin-producing sweat gland carcinoma (EMPSGC) of the eyelid, initially misdiagnosed as a chalazion.

A 76-year-old South-Asian male presented with a 9-month history of a painless left upper eyelid lesion. Initial ophthalmic assessment suggested presence of a chalazion that did not resolve with medical management. Examination revealed a 5.5 × 5.5 mm mass at the central left eyelid margin. The lesion transilluminated and extended over the eyelid margin, with splayed lashes but no madarosis. Histopathological examination demonstrated cribriforming glandular epithelium with extracellular mucin and synaptophysin expression, confirming EMPSGC with associated mucinous carcinoma. The patient underwent successful Mohs micrographic surgery with oculoplastic reconstruction and with no evidence of recurrence at five-month follow-up.

EMPSGC is an uncommon, low-grade adnexal neoplasm, often under-recognized due to its benign appearance. This case highlights the importance of considering EMPSGC in the differential diagnosis of persistent eyelid lesions, particularly those unresponsive to conservative treatment. Histopathologic evaluation is critical for early recognition and appropriate management of lesions.

Keywords: Endocrine mucin-producing carcinoma, Neuroendocrine, Eyelid neoplasm, Chalazion, Histopathology

## Introduction

Endocrine mucin-producing sweat gland carcinoma (EMPSGC) is a rare, low-grade adnexal neoplasm with approximately 250 cases reported in the literature.1,2 While EMPSGC can affect both genders, it is more commonly observed in middle-aged to elderly females, though cases in men have been documented.3, 4, 5, 6 The eyelid and periorbital regions are common sites for EMPSGC, where the lesion often mimics benign conditions like chalazia, resulting in delayed diagnosis.7 Additional workup to rule out a metastatic carcinoma or concurrent malignancy should be considered, particularly breast cancer given the common embryological origin of sweat and mammary glands.5,8 Immunohistochemical analysis may also aid in differentiating primary from secondary tumors, with myoepithelial cells at the tumor periphery supporting a primary cutaneous adnexal origin.5,9

This report describes a case of EMPSGC in the eyelid of a 76-year-old male that presented as a chalazion unresponsive to conservative treatment, underscoring the importance of considering EMPSGC in the differential diagnosis of persistent eyelid lesions. This case report adheres to HIPAA regulations and the ethical principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication, including accompanying photographs.

## Case report

A 76-year-old male with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and moderate nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy presented with a 9-month history of a left upper eyelid lesion. The lesion was described as painless and had remained stable in size over this period. The patient denied additional symptoms, including vision changes, discharge, or pruritus, but expressed interest in lesion removal due to its persistent nature and cosmetic concern.

The lesion was previously diagnosed as a chalazion by another ophthalmologist, and the patient had been instructed to use warm compresses. Despite consistent adherence to this regimen, no improvement was noted. The patient's past medical history was otherwise unremarkable for malignancy or dermatologic disorders. However, his family history was notable for an unspecified type of cancer in his brother.

On examination, a 5.5 × 5.5 mm mass was observed at the central left eyelid margin. The mass transilluminated and hung over the edge of the eyelid, with surrounding lashes splayed but without madarosis (Fig. 1). The remainder of his ophthalmic examination was unremarkable.

*Fig. 1: Left upper eyelid lesion at initial presentation.*

Given the atypical presentation and failure to respond to standard chalazion treatment, a biopsy was ultimately performed. Histopathological analysis revealed cribriform glandular epithelium with extracellular mucin and partial expression of synaptophysin, findings consistent with EMPSGC.10,11 Immunohistochemistry was positive for cytokeratin 7 and synaptophysin and negative for CD117 and S100, further supporting the diagnosis (Fig. 2).

*Fig. 2: (A) Hematoxylin and eosin staining displaying skin with nodules of cribiform glandular epithelium with extracellular mucin (arrow) compatible with endocrine mucin producing sweat gland carcinoma. (B) Representative section of tumor showing patchy synaptophysin staining of in situ component.*

The patient subsequently underwent Mohs micrographic surgery followed by oculoplastic reconstruction with direct closure of the left upper eyelid (Fig. 3A). A computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis was negative for underlying malignancy, further supporting a primary diagnosis of EMPSGC. At five-months post-operative follow-up, there was no evidence of recurrence, and the patient continues to be monitored for potential local recurrence (Fig. 3B).

*Fig. 3: (A) Left upper eyelid lesion after Mohs surgery and prior to oculoplastic reconstruction. (B) Left upper eyelid at one-month postoperative visit after oculoplastic reconstruction.*

## Discussion

EMPSCG is an uncommon, low-grade adnexal neoplasm first described by Flieder et al., in 1997.8 Histopathologically, EMPSGC is homologous to solid-papillary/endocrine ductal carcinoma in situ (eDCIS) of the breast and may serve as a precursor to invasive neuroendocrine type mucinous sweat gland carcinoma (MSC), also known as primary cutaneous mucinous carcinoma (PCMC). Studies have reported invasive mucinous components in 33.3 %–35.7 % of EMPSGC cases.2,9

EMPSGC most commonly presents around the seventh decade of life, with a reported female-to-male incidence ratio of 1.7:1.2,9,11 Despite its higher prevalence in females, recent years have seen an increase in reported cases among males, with a potential difference in sex distribution by ethnicity.1 Among East Asian populations, a male predominance has been observed, with 9 of the 10 reported cases occurring in males.3,12, 13, 14, 15, 16 The demographic profile of the patient in the current case is particularly notable. The patient, an elderly male of South Asian/Indian descent, represents a rare presentation, with just one other case in an Indian male documented in the literature, and that report did not include an associated invasive mucinous carcinoma as seen herein.17 While the majority of reported EMPSGC cases have occurred in Caucasians, few have been documented in individuals with darker skin pigmentation, including two reported cases in African American females.18,19 This makes our case one of the rare instances reported in an individual with Fitzpatrick Skin Type V or higher, raising questions about the true prevalence of EMPSGC across diverse racial and ethnic groups and suggesting the need for further studies to determine whether there are differences in clinical outcomes in darker-skinned individuals.

EMPSGC typically manifests as a slow-growing, painless nodule on the skin, most commonly on the eyelid or periorbital region, though other sites including the cheek and scalp may also be involved. Due to its nonspecific clinical appearance, EMPSGC can be confused with benign lesions such as cysts or chalazia, leading to delayed diagnosis and definitive treatment.7,8 The diagnostic challenges of benign-appearing lesions are highlighted by a retrospective pathological analysis of 1033 lesions initially diagnosed as chalazia which revealed a 6.4 % misdiagnosis rate, with actual diagnoses including malignant, premalignant, and other benign conditions.20 A separate case series of 11 EMPSCG patients found that 64 % were initially misdiagnosed as chalazia or hordeola.21 These findings underscore the need for heightened clinical suspicion and the importance of early histopathological evaluation for persistent or atypical lesions. Other potential causes of a persistent eyelid lesion encompass a wide differential, ranging from inflammatory to neoplastic conditions. These include benign entities such as hidradenoma, hidrocystoma, and cystadenoma, as well as malignant lesions like basal cell carcinoma. Accurate diagnosis often hinges on histopathological and immunohistochemical evaluation, given the clinical overlap among these conditions.

The diagnosis of EMPSGC relies on characteristic histopathological features and immunohistochemical profile. Histologically, EMPSGC is characterized by mucin production and neuroendocrine differentiation.10 Positive staining with chromogranin A and synaptophysin are indicative of neuroendocrine differentiation, though other emerging markers, such as insulinoma-associated protein 1, have been reported to have greater sensitivity for neuroendocrine differentiation.22 Other immunohistochemical markers such as cytokeratin 7, epithelial membrane antigen, gross cystic disease fluid protein-15, estrogen receptor, and progesterone receptor, are often positive, and cytokeratin 20 is often negative, aiding in the diagnosis.10 The presence of myoepithelial cells at the tumor periphery, highlighted by markers such as SMA, calponin, p63/p40, and S100, supports a primary cutaneous adnexal origin over metastatic carcinoma.9 This biopsy section in the case presented was positive for synaptophysin, indicating neuroendocrine differentiation, and was noted to have a mucinous carcinoma arising within the EMPSGC (Fig. 2).

Diagnostic workup includes biopsy and histopathological examination with immunohistochemistry to confirm neuroendocrine features and distinguish it from other cutaneous carcinomas. In rare instances, clinicians may consider additional investigations to rule out primary or concurrent malignancies, particularly breast cancer, due to the shared embryological and histological features of sweat and mammary glands.5,8 For instance, one case reported a 75-year-old female with EMPSGC of the lower eyelid who was found to have a concurrent low-grade, invasive ductal mucinous carcinoma of the breast. Histopathology in this case demonstrated an in situ component of the EMPSGC, establishing it as a primary cutaneous lesion rather than a metastatic tumor.23 Similarly, multiple primary carcinomas were reported in a 71-year-old woman diagnosed with two EMPSGC lesions on her face, a mucinous carcinoma of the skin, and an invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast.24 This phenomenon has also been reported in a 73-year-old male with EMPSGC who underwent systemic workup after revealing abnormal nipple discharge and was found to have an intraductal papilloma of the breast.5 The presence of multiple concurrent lesions may represent an underlying susceptibility to the development of apocrine tumors, highlighting the need for thorough systemic evaluation in patients presenting with EMPSGC.

The mainstay of treatment for EMPSGC is surgical, with Mohs micrographic surgery or other traditional surgical excision with clear margins being the preferred approaches. The prognosis for EMPSGC is generally favorable, with a low risk of recurrence or metastasis (approximately 7–8 %).1,9 Risk of recurrence is higher in EMPSGC with associated PCMC compared to those without PCMC.9 Regardless of association with PCMC, long-term follow-up is advised to monitor for potential recurrence and ensure optimal patient outcomes.

## Conclusions

This case highlights the importance of maintaining a broad differential diagnosis for eyelid lesions that are unresponsive to conservative management. While rare, EMPSGC should be considered when evaluating persistent nodules in the periorbital or facial regions, as anti-inflammatory treatments for conditions such as chalazion or hordeolum may obscure its presentation. The initiation of appropriate histopathologic and immunohistochemical investigations is critical in order to ensure timely diagnosis and treatment. Systemic workup may also be considered in select cases to exclude concurrent malignancies.

# Deep-Learning Based Automated Segmentation and Quantitative Volumetric Analysis of Orbital Muscle and Fat for Diagnosis of Thyroid Eye Disease

**Authors:** Adham M. Alkhadrawi; Lisa Y. Lin; Saul A. Langarica; Kyungsu Kim; Sierra K. Ha; Nahyoung G. Lee; Synho Do

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Radiology, Lab of Medical Imaging and Computation, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, United States | 2Department of Ophthalmology, Ophthalmic Plastic Surgery Service, Massachusetts Eye and Ear, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, United States, | 3KU-Korea Institute of Science and Technology (KIST) Graduate School of Converging Science and Technology, Korea University, Seoul, Korea | 4Kempner Institute, Harvard University, Boston, Massachusetts, United States

## Abstract

Thyroid eye disease (TED) is characterized by proliferation of orbital tissues and complicated by compressive optic neuropathy (CON). This study aims to utilize a deep-learning (DL)-based automated segmentation model to segment orbital muscle and fat volumes on computed tomography (CT) images and provide quantitative volumetric data and a machine learning (ML)-based classifier to distinguish between TED and TED with CON.

Subjects with TED who underwent clinical evaluation and orbital CT imaging were included. Patients with clinical features of CON were classified as having severe TED, and those without were classified as having mild TED. Normal subjects were used for controls. A U-Net DL-model was used for automatic segmentation of orbital muscle and fat volumes from orbital CTs, and ensemble of Random Forest Classifiers were used for volumetric analysis of muscle and fat.

Two hundred eighty-one subjects were included in this study. Automatic segmentation of orbital tissues was performed. Dice coefficient was recorded to be 0.902 and 0.921 for muscle and fat volumes, respectively. Muscle volumes among normal, mild, and severe TED were found to be statistically different. A classification model utilizing volume data and limited patient data had an accuracy of 0.838 and an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.929 in predicting normal, mild TED, and severe TED.

DL-based automated segmentation of orbital images for patients with TED was found to be accurate and efficient. An ML-based classification model using volumetrics and metadata led to high diagnostic accuracy in distinguishing TED and TED with CON. By enabling rapid and precise volumetric assessment, this may be a useful tool in future clinical studies.

Thyroid eye disease (TED) is a heterogeneous autoimmune condition that can have a varied presentation. TED can be disfiguring, and early detection can be critical to avoid permanent vision loss. Due to aberrant signaling and overactivation of thyroid stimulating hormone receptor and insulin-like growth factor-1 pathways in TED, there is abnormal growth and uncontrolled proliferation of orbital tissues.1–4 TED signs and symptoms, such as extraocular motility limitation and proptosis, are consequences to changes in the orbital fat and muscles, but diagnosis may be delayed due to its varied and nonspecific presenting symptoms. When the expansion of these tissues is severe, there may be vision-threatening complications, like compressive optic neuropathy (CON). Management and treatment strategies aim to alleviate symptoms, manage inflammation and disfigurement, and, in severe cases, prevent or address CON. However, identification of patients at risk for serious sequelae to achieve urgent triage to an oculoplastic surgeon is critical.

Volumetric segmentation is frequently utilized in radiotherapy for assessment of targeted organs and anatomic structures throughout the body. Automated segmentation of radiographic images has been a rapidly expanding field in the last decade to reduce the time and variability associated with manual segmentation utilizing techniques based on multi-atlas algorithms. Recently, deep learning (DL) has broadened the applicability of auto-segmentation and has allowed for broader generalization of new data.5 For TED, the quantification of orbital muscle and fat volumes in TED have been explored and volumetric based studies have helped better understand disease pathophysiology, corresponding clinical features, and response to therapies.6–24 However, many of these studies depend on manual segmentation for demarcation of orbital tissues of interest, which is time and labor intensive.11,13,14,25 Alternatively, they may involve the utilization of commercial or open-source software packages, many of which are programed based on normal orbital scans and may have less generalizability to patients with TED6,8,12,16,18–21 or may still require some manual segmentation. Orbital imaging of TED poses a unique challenge for segmentation and volumetric analysis due to a relatively small target organ, the irregular expansion of the orbital muscles and fat, and the apical crowding within the bony orbit.

This study aims to introduce a DL-based fully automated approach for the segmentation of orbital muscle and fat, and subsequent quantitative volume measurement using orbital computed tomography (CT) scans in patients with TED and TED with CON. This study also aims to utilize this volumetric data in a DL-based classification model and integrates patient-specific data in conjunction with the image data for optimized classification.

## Methods

### Study Design

A retrospective cohort study was performed at Massachusetts Eye and Ear (MEE), a tertiary ophthalmic institution, over a 12-year period (August 2011 to 2023). The Massachusetts General Brigham (MGB) institutional review board approved this retrospective study, and the written informed consent was waived. The study was conducted following the ethical standards outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki and conducted in compliance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act.

Subject identification methods were previously described.26 Subjects were included if they were 18 years of age or older with a dedicated CT scan of the orbit who had also undergone a clinical examination by an oculoplastic surgeon within a 3-month period of the scan. Patients with a clinical diagnosis of TED were included. Patients with no TED or other orbital conditions who underwent CT orbits were included as normal controls. Patients were excluded if they had another orbital diagnosis, such as orbital tumors, fractures, or other inflammatory processes, and patients with any prior orbital surgery (e.g. orbital decompressions).

A multi-faceted approach to the DL algorithm was constructed, with an overview of the study methodology presented in Figure 1. First, the region of interest (ROI) was extracted (see Fig. 1, stage 1) from the orbital CTs, with details on methodology to follow. DL-based segmentation was then performed to segment muscle and fat volumes of each orbit (see Fig. 1, stage 2). Calculation of orbital muscle and orbital fat volumes were then performed. Then, the volumetric data was processed in synergy with patient metadata through a DL-based classifier to predict the presence of normal, mild TED, or severe TED (see Fig. 1, stage 3).

*Figure 1.: Overview of the proposed DL volumetric analysis methodology. In stage 1, the input whole CT scan is automatically cropped to extract right and left orbits. In stage 2, DL-based automated segmentation of the muscle and fat volumes in each orbit is performed and the volumes of each are subsequently calculated. In stage 3, the volumetric data is integrated with various patient metadata into an ML-based classifier which is used to diagnosis the patient with normal, mild TED, or severe TED.*

### Data Preprocessing

#### Patient Metadata Collection and Categorization

Patient demographics, clinical history, smoking status, ancillary testing, and oculoplastic surgeon's clinical examination closest in time to the CT were abstracted from the electronic medical record. Based on retrospective chart review, patients were categorized into three groups: normal patients, patients with mild TED (no optic neuropathy), and patients with severe TED (with optic neuropathy), as previously described.26 Patients with severe TED were considered to have any signs of compressive optic neuropathy, including any one of the following: dyschromatopsia, Humphrey visual field (VF) changes in patterns consistent with TED, relative afferent pupillary defect, and/or optic nerve head changes.27 Optic nerve head changes were identified on direct fundoscopic examination and including optic, and documented if there was any blurring of disc margins, disc edema, or disc pallor. These clinical categories were deemed the ground truth for model training.

#### Computed Tomography Data (CT Scans) Preprocessing

Orbital CTs from selected subjects were obtained. The slice thickness of the scans was 0.625 mm, and the pixel dimensions were 512 × 512 pixels. To maximize the clarity of the orbit, the image volume was clipped to 1000 pixels window level and 350 pixels window width. After this windowing process, each individual orbit (right and left orbit) was cropped to a 140 × 140 × 140-pixel volume. The right and left orbits of each CT scan were cropped by a fixed-size ROI. The orbital structures were not affected by the slight shifts in the ROI positions because all CT scans had the same pixel dimensions (512 × 512 pixels). This proof-of-concept model did not create a general cropping method that could handle different CT scan sizes and offsets. The cropped volumes of a subset of images were then manually segmented by experienced radiologists utilizing FIJI software and Labkit.28,29 The manual segmentations of these orbits were performed to establish the ground truth for subsequent model training. The total number of manually segmented slices was 4200, which was split into three sets: training (3360), validation (420), and testing (420). The obtained segmentation masks of orbital muscles and fat were stored separately for model training. The dataset was divided into training, validation, and test sets, with the allocation ratios being 80%, 10%, and 10%, respectively.

### Model Development

#### Orbital Volume Segmentation Model

A 2D U-Net30 model was utilized for segmentation tasks. The adapted U-Net architecture featured an encoder-decoder design, with the encoder module utilizing a pretrained VGG16 model31 for feature extraction from the processed CT volumes. The decoder module comprised an equivalent number of layers. During the training process, a learning rate of 1e-4 and a batch size of 4 were applied over 100 epochs, utilizing the cross-entropy loss function. To enhance dataset diversity and enhance the model's overall performance, normalization and resizing transforms were implemented as augmentation techniques during training. The following augmentation techniques were used: (a) rotation (limit = 50 degrees, probability = 1.0), (b) horizontal flip (probability = 0.5), and (c) vertical flip (probability = 0.5). Slices were then resized to 160 × 160 pixels for the purpose of training as the library “Segmentation Models Pytorch” (https://github.com/qubvel/segmentation_models.pytorch) required image height and width to be multiples of 32. The Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) was used as a metric to assess the model's accuracy, calculated through the following formula (Equation 1: ( A , B ) = 2 ( A ∩ B ) ( A + B ) ). The output of the segmentation model includes both a 3-dimensional (3D) volumetric model as well as quantifications of the muscle volumes and fat volumes for each orbit. To assess the performance of the segmentation models, the model was applied to the test set data. A Monte Carlo five-fold cross-validation with data randomly shuffled was performed. The averaged DSC was then calculated.

We applied a post-processing step to resize the predicted masks back to their original 140 × 140 pixel dimensions to ensure accurate volume calculation. The muscle and fat volumes were calculated for each orbit by multiplying voxel volume (dx,.dy, and.dz) by the predicted mask area (nmask) for each slice in the volume (Equation 2: V3D = nmask · (dx · dy · dz)) and then compared for each classification (normal, mild TED, and severe TED) as well as subclassification based on male and female gender. Statistical comparison on outcomes was performed with 1-way ANOVA testing.

#### TED Classification Model

After the volumes were automatically segmented, an ML-based model was developed for classification of the images. The classification model utilized a Random Forest model design to classify among the three groups (normal, mild TED, and severe TED). The classification approach is represented in Figure 2. The input for the model was the predicted orbital muscle and orbital fat volumes obtained from the segmentation model. The input was then run through the ML-based classifier, which predicts the probability of each image belonging to each class in a binary fashion (i.e. normal versus not normal, mild TED versus not mild TED, and severe TED versus not severe TED). Finally, the output of the three binary models is combined into a voting scheme, which predicts the final classification of each case (normal versus mild TED versus severe TED).

*Figure 2.: TED classification methodology. Three binary models, one for each class, was implemented. Each model outputs the estimated probability that the instance belongs to the corresponding class, and then the voting module decides the final class of the input instance based on these probabilities, ultimately predicting the diagnosis.*

This classification model was also re-run in synergy with several different combinations of patient metadata, following similar model structure as demonstrated in Figure 2. The aim was to identify the minimal set of input variables to achieve the highest accuracy of prediction and overall performance. The initial classification model utilizing only volumetric data was called model 1 (M1). The second model (M2) only applied features from the patient's metadata, including demographic and clinical examination data as measured by an oculoplastic surgeon. The third model (M3) utilized all features from M1 and M2. The fourth model (M4) used volumetrics and some patient metadata that could be easily assessed without an oculoplastic examination (patient age, gender, race, and smoking status). Supplementary Table S1 lists all input variables for the four models. The accuracy and area under the curve (AUC) for all four model combinations was calculated, with outcomes for each binary model (i.e. normal versus not normal, mild TED versus not mild TED, and severe TED versus not Severe TED) and the main model (normal versus mild TED versus severe TED).

In order to pursue explainable artificial intelligence (AI) outcomes, feature importance of the Random Forest classifiers was also performed. The features analyzed include age, gender, race, smoking status, orbital muscle volumes, orbital fat volumes, and total orbital volumes. The impurity importance or the Gini importance32 of all the input variables was calculated. Partial Dependence Plots (PDPs)33 were also used to inspect the independent effects of all the input variables on the decisions of the classifiers.

### Orbital Volume Segmentation Results and Analysis

The orbital fat and muscle volume segmentation model underwent training and was tested on 10% of the data. Representative examples of the DL-based auto-segmentation model results are shown in Figure 3 and the Supplementary Figures S1–S3. The model successfully took an input image of the CT orbit, identified, and segmented the muscle and fat within the orbit, generated a 3D volumetric model, and calculated the respective volumes of the muscle and fat of each orbit for patients with normal, mild TED, and severe TED.

The performance was cross-validated on the remaining 10% of the data using a 5-fold cross-validation with random shuffling of the data. The DSC of the muscle volumes had an average of 0.902 (0.882, 0.913, 0.906, 0.896, and 0.912 for each round of cross-validation split, respectively). The DSC of the fat volumes had an average of 0.921 (0.941, 0.922, 0.904, 0.924, and 0.908 for each round of cross-validation split, respectively).

### TED Classification Results and Analysis

After the volumes of the muscle and fat of the orbit were calculated for all the cases, the TED classification model was used to classify each case into one of the three categories, namely, normal versus mild TED versus severe TED, using the composition of the three binary models (see Fig. 2). One notable advantage of training the binary models independently was that the strong class imbalance present in the data could be easily mitigated. For example, when training the binary model mild versus not mild, the not mild class included both the normal and severe cases, and for the mild class, only an equivalent number of cases were considered. The same procedure was followed to train the other binary models.

The data were divided into training, validation, and testing with corresponding ratios of 0.6, 0.2, and 0.2, respectively. The training and validation sets were used for hyperparameter optimization of the model, and the hyperparameters of the best performing model were used to classify the cases in the test set. The classification was performed on fat and muscle volumes calculated for both eyes as an average of the respective volumes for each patient.

The accuracy and AUC over the test set of each variation of the model are as follows. The M1 model (volume data only) had an accuracy of 0.720 and an AUC of 0.874 in predicting the main outcome between normal versus mild TED versus severe TED. The M2 model (patient metadata only) had an accuracy of 0.795 and an AUC of 0.831 in predicting the main outcome. The M3 model (M1 and M2 data combined) had an accuracy of 0.828 and an AUC of 0.903 in predicting the main outcome. The M4 model (volume data and limited patient data) had the highest accuracy of 0.838 and an AUC of 0.929 in predicting the main outcome. The receiver operator curve (ROC) for the three binary models in M4 is presented in Figure 4.

## Discussion

This study presents a DL model that can automatically segment the orbital muscle and fat volumes based on orbital CTs. The volumetric data analysis found orbital muscle volumes were significantly different with increasing volumes among normal, mild TED, and severe TED. Additionally, this study utilizes an ML-based classification model using a combination of volumetric data and patient metadata. The M4 model (volumetric data + limited patient data) was found to be the most accurate in distinguishing among all three categories (normal versus mild TED versus severe TED).

The orbital volume segmentation model was able to segment the orbital muscle and fat volumes accurately and efficiently. When the model is used, it can obtain the volumetric data from the orbital CTs rapidly, with both segmentation and quantitative volume results in approximately 30 seconds or less. It was also found to be highly accurate in cross-validation, with an average DSC of 0.902 and 0.921 for muscle and fat volumes, respectively. The slightly higher accuracy for the fat volume segmentation may be attributed to the lower density of fat tissue in Hounsfield Units compared to orbital muscle or globe, which may allow for the model to distinguish the fat more easily from surrounding tissues. The volumetric outcomes were subanalyzed by gender. The average orbital muscle volumes for normal, mild TED, and severe TED, respectively, were found to be 3.21 ± 0.95, 4.34 ± 1.39, and 5.42 ± 0.83 cm3 for male patients and 3.50 ± 0.47, 4.46 ± 1.29, and 5.94 ± 2.19 cm3 for female patients, similar to values determined in other studies.12,22

There was significant variation in muscle volumes across the three categories (P < 0.0003), with a notable progressive increase in volumes from normal healthy patients to patients with mild and severe TED, in alignment with muscle volume changes in other studies.7,9,20 In contrast, the average orbital fat volumes were statistically significant for normal, mild TED, and severe TED for male patients (P < 0.003), but not for female patients. The fat volumes also did not progressively increase, and the patients with mild TED trended toward having higher fat volumes than patients with severe TED.

There is variability in orbital fat and muscle volume in the literature for “normal” orbits, likely driven by variations in age, gender, and ethnicity.18,34–37 Other investigations of orbital muscle and fat volumes in patients with TED specifically have both a wide range of methodology and results. Some investigations on orbital volumes were based on manual segmentations of orbital imaging.11,13,14,22,25 In 1982, Feldon and Weiner provided some of the first quantitative volumetric data based on manual tracings of orbital tissues on CT for eight patients with TED.22 They similarly found a regular increase in extraocular muscle volume with worsening severity of TED. In 1982, a more automated approach was developed utilizing region-growing and automatic tracing algorithms as early attempts to measure orbital tissue volumes on CT for patients with TED.7 However, this program still required moderate additional effort and manual data processing. They found comparable measurements in healthy individuals to this study. Commercial and open-source software packages provide tools for manual or semi-automated segmentation of 3D images that have aided volumetric studies in TED.8,12,18–20 Some of these studies have explored correlation of volumetric data to clinical data, such as correlation between the orbital muscle volumes to vertical strabismus,8 or the predictive potential of orbital muscle volume in diagnosing CON, identifying the medial rectus muscle volume as the most robust predictor.12 Other studies utilized magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to assess orbital volumes.6,17,24,34,38–40 One study utilized a semi-automatic approach for segmenting orbital muscles in TED using MRIs and found a substantial reduction in time, from 20 minutes for the manual segmentation to 7 minutes.17 Although MRIs are higher resolution, they are more costly and time intensive compared to CTs. For TED diagnosis and management, CTs are usually sufficient and generally the imaging modality of choice. Therefore, this study utilized CTs to improve generalizability and provide a more real-world accessible tool.

With the expansion of DL based volumetric studies in radiology, the integration of DL techniques has been applied to the study of TED as well. Jiang et al. presented a study on DL-based FCN-8s network derived auto-segmentation model for CTs to determine the clinical target volumes for potential radiotherapy, a region which includes the soft tissues within the bony orbit posterior to the globe. They found the DL-based model was similar to manual contouring, but they did not segment orbital fat and muscles separately. Another study utilizing a DL-based technique using Semantic V-Net was developed for the automated segmentation and volume measurement of orbital muscles of 97 presumably predominantly Chinese patients, with an overall Intersection over Union (IOU) score of 0.8207.23 This study provides similar automatic segmentation tools with training across a broader cohort of patients, with a DSC of 0.902.

The segmentation and volume extraction data were subsequently utilized to correlate radiographic findings with a clinical diagnosis. The M1 model utilized volume data alone and was moderately accurate at distinguishing among normal, mild TED, and severe TED (accuracy of 0.720 and AUC of 0.874). The M2 model with patient clinical data and no volumetric data demonstrated similar results (accuracy of 0.795 and AUC of 0.831), and the M3 model which combined all the data from M1 and M2 mode further improved the accuracy in distinguishing all three categories (accuracy of 0.828 and AUC of 0.903). However, the patient clinical data in M2 and M3 are clinical measurements obtained by the oculoplastic surgeon, and included features such as lagophthalmos, and inferior and superior scleral show. In order for a model to be generalizable and easily adoptable, it was felt that the clinical features that are integrated into the model should be easily assessed by a non-ophthalmology trained provider. Thus, M4 included volume data and limited patient data (age, gender, race, and smoking history). Interestingly, the pared down clinical data in synergy with the volumetric data was the most accurate model (accuracy of 0.838 and AUC of 0.929) in distinguishing the three categories. This model may be capturing the heterogeneity in which TED is manifested across different age, gender, and race, and thus improving the model accuracy. Given that the M4 model had the best overall performance and no reliance on ophthalmic expertise, this model was felt to be the best use in practice and all subsequent analysis was based on this model.

Additional analysis was performed to better understand the decision making in the ML model. Explainable DL models provide human-interpretable explanations for the model decisions.41,42 Although it is not always clear what ML-based models emphasize, it is important to explore the features that the model emphasizes in order to provide transparency for the model, which is critical for healthcare implementation. On feature importance analysis, orbital muscle volume was determined to be the most important feature in distinguishing normal healthy patients and patients with severe TED, whereas orbital fat volume, followed closely by orbital muscle volume, total orbital volume, and age, was the most important feature for patients with mild TED.

The strengths of this study include its large cohort of patients, and that the volumetric DL model was trained on both normal healthy patients and patients with TED, which allows for higher accuracy in future TED studies. Volume analysis and segmentation in patients with TED is particularly challenging due to the small confined bony space and crowding at the apex. By training the model on patients with TED rather than a normal cohort alone, the segmentation and volume analysis is more adaptable to the heterogeneity of TED orbital tissues on imaging and improvement in accuracy of measurements. This study was also performed on CTs rather than MRIs, which is more clinically applicable in the real-world. However, this study also has several limitations to consider. As this was a single-centered study, the patient demographic is skewed toward Caucasian patients and may make the model less generalizable in various patient demographics. Additionally, this model only included normal or TED CT scans, and excluded those with other orbital processes or prior surgeries. This again limits the model's generalizability and utility in implementation. In addition, the use of volume data obtained from the segmentation model to train the classification model might introduce some bias, however, we assume that the characteristics of the data differ significantly between the images and the calculated volumes, which we believed would mitigate the risk of bias. Last, the imaging analysis was performed retrospectively and subjects were not required to have fixation targets, which may lead to variation in axis of segmentation or contraction states of the muscle. However, this is more applicable to real-world utilization where subjects are routinely getting imaging. Future studies include applying the model to different patient cohorts, with a more diverse patient demographic, for further optimization and validation. Comparison of this model to the accuracy of human graders, including radiologists and oculoplastic surgeons, should also be explored.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates an accurate and efficient model that automatically segments and precisely calculates the orbital fat and muscle volumes in under thirty seconds. This provides high-quality, quantitative data in analyzing the orbital soft tissues for patients with TED in a rapid fashion. This volumetric model was then utilized to provide precise quantitative volumetric data to build a highly accurate classification model for predicting the presence of TED and TED with CON. The model also synergistically used patient clinical information to optimize the classification accuracy. With further validation, this model may serve as a platform for future clinical studies and real-time incorporation into clinical practice and triage. Overall, this tool may have potential to enhance patient care through supporting broader radiographic based clinical research.
